titulo_es: Zero and second conditionals (general truths and unreal situations)
descripcion_es: If + present for general truths; if + past + would for hypothetical situations in the present.
resumen: The zero conditional expresses what always happens if a condition is met. The second conditional expresses imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or the future.

filas: If you heat ice, it melts.
If I had more time, I would learn Chinese.

explicacion.texto: In the zero conditional if is almost the same as when: whenever A happens, B happens (scientific laws, routines, instructions). In the second conditional, the past does not show past time but unreality: Spanish “Si tuviera más tiempo, aprendería chino” (If I had more time, I would learn Chinese).

items: Never put would in the if part: If I knew (not If I would know).
With be, were is preferred for all persons, especially in careful style: If I were you, I'd accept the offer.
Instead of would you can use could or might: If we had a car, we could visit them.
The order can be reversed; there is no comma when if comes second: I'd travel more if I had money.

explicacion.texto: First versus second: If I win the lottery (I see it as possible) versus If I won the lottery (I see it as unlikely or imaginary).

ejemplos.frase: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
ejemplos.traduccion: Si mezclas azul y amarillo, obtienes verde.

ejemplos.frase: If I don't sleep enough, I get a headache.
ejemplos.traduccion: Si no duermo lo suficiente, me duele la cabeza.

ejemplos.frase: If I were you, I would talk to her.
ejemplos.traduccion: Yo que tú, hablaría con ella.

ejemplos.frase: What would you do if you found a wallet in the street?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Qué harías si encontraras una cartera en la calle?

ejemplos.frase: If we lived closer to the sea, we could go swimming every day.
ejemplos.traduccion: Si viviéramos más cerca del mar, podríamos ir a nadar todos los días.

ejemplos.frase: She wouldn't be so tired if she went to bed earlier.
ejemplos.traduccion: No estaría tan cansada si se acostara antes.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: If I would have money, I would buy a house.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: If I had money, I would buy a house.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The if part takes the past simple, not would (Spanish uses the subjunctive “tuviera”).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: If I was you, I'd study more.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: If I were you, I'd study more.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The fixed expression for giving advice is If I were you; was is informal and is avoided in an exam.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: If you will press this button, the machine stops.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: If you press this button, the machine stops.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: In the zero conditional both parts are in the present simple.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form (zero conditional).
respuestas: boil
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the zero conditional from the table: If + present simple, present simple. The clue is the other part of the sentence, it evaporates, in the present simple, and the fact that it describes a physical law that is always true. With the subject you, the present simple is the base form: boil.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will boil
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will does not go after if; in the zero conditional both parts are in the present simple.

errores_previstos.respuesta: boils
errores_previstos.explicacion: With the subject you the present has no -s; the -s is only for he, she, it.

errores_previstos.respuesta: boiled
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past would turn the sentence into a hypothesis (second conditional), and it would not fit with evaporates.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form (zero conditional).
ejercicios.frase: Plants die if they ___ (not get) enough light.
respuestas: don't get
do not get
ejercicios.explicacion: Zero conditional again: present simple in both parts, because it is a general truth about plants. The clue is die, in the present, and the subject they (plants). The negative of the present simple with they is formed with don't (do not) + base verb: don't get. Both forms, contracted and full, are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Zero conditional: present simple in both parts.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las plantas mueren si no reciben suficiente luz.

errores_previstos.respuesta: doesn't get
errores_previstos.explicacion: Doesn't is for he, she, it; the subject is they (the plants), which requires don't.

errores_previstos.respuesta: not get
errores_previstos.explicacion: In English the negative of the present needs the auxiliary do: don't get.

errores_previstos.respuesta: won't get
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will is not used after if; the zero conditional takes the present simple.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form (second conditional).
ejercicios.frase: If I ___ (have) a garden, I would grow tomatoes.
respuestas: had
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the second conditional from the table: If + past simple, would + infinitive. The clue is would grow in the other part, which marks an unreal hypothesis (I don't have a garden). That is why the past simple had goes after if; here it does not show past time but unreality, like Spanish “tuviera”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si tuviera un jardín, plantaría tomates.

errores_previstos.respuesta: would have
errores_previstos.explicacion: The card forbids it: never put would in the if part.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present would make a first conditional (I see it as possible) and would not fit with would grow.

errores_previstos.respuesta: had had
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past perfect belongs to the third conditional (unreal past); here the hypothesis is in the present.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form (second conditional).
ejercicios.frase: If she spoke German, she ___ (apply) for the job in Munich.
respuestas: would apply
'd apply
could apply
might apply
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the second part of the second conditional: would + infinitive. The clue is the condition If she spoke German, in the past simple, which shows an unreal hypothesis. Would apply and its contraction 'd apply are correct, and so are could apply (possibility) and might apply (perhaps), which the card allows instead of would.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si hablara alemán, solicitaría el puesto en Múnich.

errores_previstos.respuesta: will apply
errores_previstos.explicacion: Will belongs to the first conditional (If she speaks…); with spoke in the if part you need would.

errores_previstos.respuesta: applied
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past simple goes in the if part, not in the result part.

errores_previstos.respuesta: would applied
errores_previstos.explicacion: After would comes the infinitive without to: would apply.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of be.
ejercicios.frase: If I ___ you, I would take the train.
respuestas: were
ejercicios.explicacion: The card gives the fixed expression for advice: If I were you. With be, the second conditional prefers were for all persons, including I. The clue is would take in the other part and the meaning of advice. Was is heard in speech, but in this formula it is avoided in an exam.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed advice formula: If I were you.
ejercicios.traduccion: Yo que tú, cogería el tren.

errores_previstos.respuesta: was
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is informal; the card says that the fixed expression for giving advice is If I were you and that was is avoided in an exam.

errores_previstos.respuesta: am
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present does not express unreality: I am not you, so it is were.

errores_previstos.respuesta: would be
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would does not go in the if part.

ejercicios.frase: What ___ you do if you lost your passport abroad?
respuestas: would
ejercicios.explicacion: It is a second conditional in question form: what + would + subject + infinitive + if + past simple. The clue is lost, in the past simple inside the if clause, which presents an imaginary situation. That is why the main part requires would, not will.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Qué harías si perdieras el pasaporte en el extranjero?

por_opcion.will: Incorrect: will belongs to the first conditional (if you lose); with lost you need would.
por_opcion.would: Correct: second conditional, the hypothetical result of an imaginary situation.
por_opcion.do: Incorrect: “What do you do if…” would be a zero conditional (what you always do whenever…), and it does not fit with lost.

ejercicios.frase: If it ___ below zero, water freezes.
respuestas: gets
ejercicios.explicacion: It is a natural law, so the zero conditional is used: present simple in both parts. The clue is freezes, in the present simple, in the other half of the sentence. With the subject it the present takes -s: gets.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si la temperatura baja de cero, el agua se congela.

por_opcion.gets: Correct: present simple in the if clause, as the zero conditional requires.
por_opcion.got: Incorrect: the past would make a second conditional, which does not fit with freezes.
por_opcion.would get: Incorrect: would never goes in the if part.

ejercicios.frase: We could go to the beach if it ___ so cold.
respuestas: wasn't
ejercicios.explicacion: It is a second conditional with could in the main part, as the card allows. The clue is could go, which describes something that is not going to happen because it is cold now: unreality in the present. After if comes the past simple, wasn't; weren't, which is not among the options, would also be correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Unreal in the present: if + past simple (weren't would also be correct).
ejercicios.traduccion: Podríamos ir a la playa si no hiciera tanto frío.

por_opcion.isn't: Incorrect: the present would make a first conditional, which would require can or will, not could.
por_opcion.wasn't: Correct: past simple after if for an unreal situation in the present (weren't would also be correct).
por_opcion.wouldn't be: Incorrect: would does not go in the if part.

ejercicios.frase: If I would know the answer, I would tell you.
respuestas: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
If I knew the answer, I'd tell you.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the first mistake the card points out: never put would in the if part. The sentence has it in both halves. You must keep would only in the result and put the past simple of know in the condition: If I knew. The second part can stay as would tell or be contracted to I'd tell.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Would does not go in the if part: knew.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si supiera la respuesta, te la diría.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I would know the answer, I would tell you.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: would does not go after if.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I knew the answer, I will tell you.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The if part has been corrected, but the result of a second conditional takes would, not will.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I knowed the answer, I would tell you.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Know is irregular: its past is knew.

ejercicios.frase: If you heat butter, it would melt.
respuestas: If you heat butter, it melts.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is a general truth, so it takes the zero conditional: present simple in both parts. The clue is heat, in the present, in the condition: it is not a hypothesis but something that always happens. That is why would melt must be melts, with -s because of the subject it.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: General truth: present simple in both parts.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If you heat butter, it would melt.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: would is not used for a general truth.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If you heat butter, it melt.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With the subject it the present simple takes -s: melts.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If you heat butter, it melted.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past does not work for a general truth; in the zero conditional both parts are in the present simple.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite as a second conditional starting with “If I”.
ejercicios.frase: I don't have a car, so I can't drive to work.
respuestas: If I had a car, I could drive to work.
If I had a car, I would drive to work.
If I had a car, I'd drive to work.
If I had a car, I would be able to drive to work.
If I had a car, I'd be able to drive to work.
ejercicios.explicacion: To form a second conditional from a real situation, you reverse that situation: don't have becomes had (affirmative and in the past simple) and can't becomes could (or would). The original sentence says that I don't have a car and can't drive; the hypothesis imagines the opposite. Could drive, would drive, 'd drive and would be able to drive are all correct, because they all express the hypothetical result.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Reverse the reality: don't have → had; can't → could/would.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si tuviera coche, podría ir al trabajo en coche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I would have a car, I could drive to work.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would does not go in the if part; it takes the past simple had.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I didn't have a car, I couldn't drive to work.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It repeats the reality instead of reversing it; the hypothesis is having a car.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If I had a car, I can drive to work.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the second conditional the result takes could or would, not can.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite as a second conditional starting with “If he”.
ejercicios.frase: He isn't rich, so he doesn't travel.
respuestas: If he were rich, he would travel.
If he was rich, he would travel.
If he were rich, he'd travel.
If he was rich, he'd travel.
ejercicios.explicacion: Reverse the reality: isn't rich becomes were rich and doesn't travel becomes would travel. With be, the card prefers were for all persons, but accepts was in less careful style; that is why both are correct. The result can be written would travel or 'd travel.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Unreal in the present: if + were/was, would + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If he would be rich, he would travel.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would never goes after if; you use were (or was).

errores_previstos.respuesta: If he is rich, he would travel.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The present does not express unreality; the second conditional takes the past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If he were rich, he will travel.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The result of the second conditional takes would, not will.

respuestas: what would you do if you won
ejercicios.explicacion: It is a question in the second conditional: what + would + subject + infinitive + if + past simple. Would goes before the subject because it is a question, and won is the past simple of win, which expresses the hypothesis. The if part goes after, with no comma, as the card says when if comes second.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Hypothetical question: what would + subject + infinitive + if + past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: what you would do if you won
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a direct question the auxiliary would goes before the subject: what would you do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: if you won what you would do
errores_previstos.explicacion: Besides not inverting would and you, starting with if requires a comma and it is still not a well-formed question.

respuestas: if I were you I wouldn't go
I wouldn't go if I were you
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the fixed advice formula If I were you with wouldn't + infinitive in the result. The order can be reversed: with if first (if I were you, I wouldn't go) or second (I wouldn't go if I were you), and the card says that the comma is only needed when if comes first. That is why both orders are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Advice with If I were you + would/wouldn't.

errores_previstos.respuesta: if I wouldn't go I were you
errores_previstos.explicacion: Wouldn't goes in the result, not after if; the condition is if I were you.

errores_previstos.respuesta: if you were I I wouldn't go
errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed formula is If I were you, not the other way round.

descripcion_larga_es: The zero conditional expresses what always happens if a condition is met (If you heat ice, it melts), and the second conditional, imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or the future (If I had time, I would learn Chinese). They are basic for reasoning, giving advice and making hypotheses. They are hard for Spanish speakers because they put would in the if part, copying Spanish “tuviera” or the Spanish conditional.

contexto.que_es: They are two types of conditional sentence. The zero conditional has the present simple in both parts and describes general truths, laws or routines. The second has the past simple after if and would (or could, might) + infinitive in the other part, and describes unreal or unlikely hypotheses; the past there does not show past time but unreality.
contexto.por_que_importa: They allow you to explain causes and effects, give instructions, give advice (If I were you…) and set out hypothetical scenarios, something very common in economic analysis. Confusing them changes the message: If I win sounds possible and If I won, unlikely. Putting would after if is one of the most penalised mistakes in B1 exams.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: The zero conditional, with scientific facts, rules and processes (if you heat…, if you press…). The second, with wishes, advice and assumptions contrary to present reality (if I had, if I were you). The signal is the tense after if; where Spanish uses the imperfect subjunctive (“si tuviera”), English uses the past simple (if I had), never would.
